planting.note: Set rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F; Nemagold's nematode resistance makes it a good choice for older Gulf Coast garden beds with a history of root-knot nematode.

directions: Nemagold was developed in the mid-20th century as an improved, root-knot-nematode-resistant strain within the Puerto Rico type of sweet potato, released to protect Gulf South growers from nematode damage that plagued earlier orange-fleshed varieties. The moist, deep-orange flesh and coppery-orange skin closely resemble Beauregard and Puerto Rico in flavor and texture, producing smooth, blocky roots that store and cure well. Because it tolerates the sandy, nematode-prone soils common across the Gulf Coast, Nemagold remains a dependable heirloom choice for gardeners battling nematode pressure in older vegetable beds. Set slips after the soil has warmed in late spring and let the long, warm Gulf Coast season fully mature the crop before the first fall frost.

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost when soil is reliably warm above 65°F; Averre's root-knot nematode resistance makes it well suited to sandy, nematode-prone Gulf Coast soils where sweet potatoes are grown repeatedly.

directions: Averre was released by North Carolina State University's sweetpotato breeding program and named for plant nematologist Kenneth R. Averre, reflecting its strong resistance to root-knot nematode, a major limiting pest in sandy Southern soils. It produces moist, orange flesh and rose-copper skin similar in eating quality to Jewel and Beauregard, with smooth, uniform, fusiform roots well suited to fresh-market and home use. Averre performs reliably in the hot, humid conditions of the Gulf Coast growing season and is a good rotation option for gardeners working nematode-infested ground. Cure roots at warm temperatures and high humidity for about a week after harvest to develop full sweetness and improve storage life.

planting.note: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil is warm above 65°F; Ruddy grows vigorously through a full Gulf Coast summer and rewards a long season with heavy yields.

directions: Ruddy is a fresh-market sweet potato released by North Carolina State University's breeding program, selected for its notably darker, deeper rose-red skin than Jewel or Beauregard, which makes it stand out visually at market and in home harvests. The flesh is moist, deep orange, and sweet, with smooth, uniform roots and good resistance to several common sweetpotato diseases. It grows vigorously in the long, hot Gulf Coast season and produces heavily from a modest planting of slips. Harvest before soil temperatures drop in fall and cure promptly to bring out its full sweetness and deepen the skin color further.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost, or January-February in zone 9, 4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil; Irish Cobbler's quick maturity fits neatly into a Gulf Coast winter growing window before summer heat arrives.

directions: Irish Cobbler is one of the oldest potato varieties still grown in North America, dating to the late 19th century and long valued as one of the earliest potatoes to reach harvestable size. The round-to-irregular tubers have thin, buff-tan skin with shallow eyes and dense white flesh that is excellent for boiling, mashing, and creaming, though it does not store as long as later-maturing varieties. Because it matures quickly, Irish Cobbler is a good fit for a Gulf Coast winter-planted potato crop that needs to finish before summer heat arrives. Plant certified seed pieces in late winter and hill the developing plants as they grow to keep tubers covered and prevent greening.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost, or January-February in zone 9; Onaway's very early maturity lets Gulf Coast gardeners harvest new potatoes well before summer heat sets in.

directions: Onaway was released by Michigan State University in the 1950s and remains prized among home growers as one of the earliest potatoes available, often ready for new potatoes within about ten weeks of planting. The round, white-skinned tubers have shallow eyes and white flesh with good flavor, best used fresh rather than for long-term storage. Its rapid maturity makes Onaway a strong choice for a quick Gulf Coast spring crop planted in late winter, allowing harvest well before the region's summer heat sets in. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to protect the shallow-set tubers from sunlight and pests.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces as soon as the soil can be worked in late winter; Caribe tolerates warmer soil better than most potatoes, making it a favorite early variety for Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Caribe is an early-season potato notable for its striking purple-pink skin over pure white flesh, and for tolerating warmer soil temperatures better than many other potato varieties, which has made it a long-time favorite among Southern gardeners. The moist, waxy flesh holds its shape well after cooking, making Caribe well suited to potato salad and roasting. Its quick maturity and heat tolerance are especially useful in zone 9, where potatoes must be planted early and harvested before the ground becomes too warm for good tuber set. Plant seed pieces as early as the soil can be worked in late winter and hill regularly as the vigorous vines grow.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost, or January-February in zone 9, well ahead of the longer maturity window; hill regularly to prevent sunburned, green shoulders before summer heat arrives.

directions: Russet Norkotah was released by North Dakota State University in 1987 and quickly became one of the most widely grown russet potatoes in North America, prized for its uniform, oblong tubers, attractive netted brown skin, and consistent yields. The dry, fluffy white flesh is a classic baking and frying russet that holds up well in storage after curing. Though bred for the northern Plains, it can adapt to a Gulf Coast winter-planted crop if seed pieces go in early enough to mature before summer heat arrives. Hill the plants as they grow to prevent sunburned, green-shouldered tubers and harvest once the vines die back.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost, or January-February in zone 9; Warba's very short season lets Gulf Coast gardeners dig new potatoes well ahead of summer heat and humidity.

directions: Warba was developed at the University of Minnesota and released in the 1930s, valued ever since as an exceptionally early, reliable red-skinned potato for gardeners who want new potatoes as soon as possible after planting. The round tubers have light red skin and white flesh with good flavor, best eaten fresh since Warba does not store as well as later-season varieties. Its very short season makes it a practical option for a Gulf Coast spring potato crop planted in late winter, since it can be dug well before summer heat and humidity set in. Hill soil around the base of the plants as they grow to protect the shallow tubers and increase yield.
